summary.name: Making On-Call Not Suck
summary.one_liner: A first-person account by Molly Struve of how Kenna split a single, miserable on-call rotation into three team-owned rotations to improve ownership, reduce SRE burnout, and speed up incident response.
use_cases: Redesigning an on-call rotation for a growing engineering team
Assigning code and alert ownership across dev teams
Reducing SRE team burnout from constant on-call escalations
Using CODEOWNERS to route pull request reviews to owning teams
Improving alert quality by handing alerts to the teams that own them
summary.what_it_does: This is an essay describing how Kenna restructured its on-call process. A single rotation covering every developer was split into three rotations, one per dev team, so each developer went on call more often. Background workers, service alerts, and application components of a shared Rails monolith were divided among the three teams. The SRE team walked each team through its assigned code, and GitLab's CODEOWNERS file was used to tag owners on pull requests touching their files. The article also moved customer-communication decisions from on-call devs to the support team and made the on-call devs act as fallbacks for each other rather than relying on SRE.
notable: Splits one on-call rotation into three team-owned rotations with clear ownership of workers, alerts, and Rails components
Uses GitLab's CODEOWNERS file to automatically tag owning teams for review on PRs
Moves status page and customer messaging decisions from on-call devs to the support team
Reports improved alerting, faster incident response, and less SRE burnout after the change
caveats: Describes one company's experience in a single monolithic Rails app; results may not transfer directly to other organizations
Gives no quantitative metrics for alert accuracy or response times; benefits are described qualitatively
